The great livestock market and meatpacking district of Chicago, opened on Christmas Day 1865 and closed in 1971. Railroads brought cattle, hogs and sheep from the West into its pens, and for decades it was the largest meatpacking centre in the world.

Packers such as Armour and Swift built a "disassembly line", where carcasses moved past rows of workers who each made one cut. Henry Ford later said the idea helped inspire his assembly line. Swift's ice-cooled railway cars, from the late 1870s, let fresh beef be shipped east instead of live animals. That changed how America ate and drove down meat prices.

Work in the yards was dangerous and poorly paid, done mostly by immigrants. In 1906 Upton Sinclair's novel The Jungle exposed the filth and cruelty there. Public disgust led to the first US federal food safety and meat inspection laws the same year.

As trucks and new plants near the ranches took over, the yards declined. Today little is left but the old stone gate.
